clinicalPearls: A narrowing of the aorta, most often just distal to the left subclavian artery near the ductal region, obstructing flow to the lower body.
The hallmark examination finding is diminished, delayed, or absent femoral pulses compared with the upper limbs, with a blood pressure gradient higher in the arms than the legs.
Severe coarctation may be duct-dependent in the neonate: as the ductus arteriosus closes, lower-body perfusion falls, producing shock, acidosis, and heart failure.
A prostaglandin infusion is used to reopen or maintain ductal patency and restore lower-body perfusion while stabilising a critically ill neonate before repair.
Older children may be asymptomatic and present with an incidentally found murmur, upper-limb hypertension, headaches, or leg claudication.
Coarctation is commonly associated with a bicuspid aortic valve and may occur with other left-sided obstructive lesions and Turner syndrome.
Chest radiograph in older children can show rib notching from collateral vessels and a figure-3 aortic contour.
Echocardiography defines the site and severity of narrowing and associated lesions; CT or MR angiography is useful for detailed anatomy.
Repair by surgery or catheter intervention relieves the obstruction, but lifelong follow-up is needed for recoarctation and persistent hypertension.
reference.pathophysiology: A discrete or long-segment narrowing of the aortic lumen creates a mechanical obstruction to systemic outflow. Proximal to the obstruction, pressure rises, producing upper-body hypertension and left ventricular pressure overload; distal to it, perfusion pressure falls, causing weak lower-body pulses. In severe neonatal coarctation, lower-body perfusion depends on right-to-left flow through the ductus arteriosus, so ductal closure precipitates hypoperfusion, metabolic acidosis, and circulatory collapse. In slowly progressive disease, collateral arterial channels develop to bypass the obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Essential hypertension in an older child
additionalInvestigations: Four-limb blood pressure measurement and simultaneous upper- and lower-limb pulse assessment
Echocardiography to define coarctation site, severity, and associated lesions such as bicuspid valve
Chest radiograph for rib notching and aortic contour in older children
CT or MR angiography for detailed arch anatomy
Assessment for acidosis and end-organ perfusion in the collapsing neonate
redFlags: Neonatal circulatory collapse with shock and acidosis as the ductus arteriosus closes in duct-dependent coarctation
Absent or markedly weak femoral pulses with an upper-to-lower limb blood pressure gradient
Signs of heart failure and poor lower-body perfusion in an infant
Severe upper-limb hypertension with headaches or hypertensive complications
Evidence of end-organ hypoperfusion such as oliguria or feeding intolerance
reference.prognosis: Early repair of significant coarctation gives a good outlook, but patients need lifelong surveillance for recoarctation, residual or late hypertension, aneurysm formation, and associated valve disease. Unrecognised severe neonatal coarctation can be rapidly fatal.
pitfalls: Failing to palpate femoral pulses and compare limb blood pressures in an unwell neonate or hypertensive child
Missing a duct-dependent coarctation until the neonate collapses as the ductus closes
Attributing upper-limb hypertension in a child to essential hypertension without checking for a gradient
Overlooking associated bicuspid aortic valve and other left-sided lesions
Assuming successful repair eliminates the need for ongoing hypertension and recoarctation surveillance
